## Introduction

Feeding competition has been considered one of the most important links between ecological factors and the social organization of gregarious species[1](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR1 "van Schaik, C. P. The ecology of social relationships amongst female primates in Comparative socioecology: the behavioural ecology of humans and other mammals (eds Standon, V. & Foley, R. A.) 195–218 (Blackwell Scientific Publications, Oxford, 1989)."),[2](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR2 "Clutton-Brock, T. & Janson, C. Primate socioecology at the crossroads: Past, present, and future. Evol. Anthropol. 21, 136–150 (2012)."). Socioecological models predict that ecological factors primarily determine the foraging efficiency, reproductive success, and distribution of females; which in turn will influence the distribution of males[3](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR3 "Kappeler, P. M. & van Schaik, C. P. Evolution of primate social systems. Int. J. Primatol. 23, 707–740 (2002)."),[4](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR4 "Koenig, A., Scarry, C. J., Wheeler, B. C. & Borries, C. Variation in grouping patterns, mating systems and social structure: what socio-ecological models attempt to explain. Phil. Trans. Roy. Soc. B 368 (2013)."). The relationships between foraging efficiency and group size can be influenced by both scramble competition and contest competition, which can occur both within groups and between groups[5](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR5 "Janson, C. H. & van Schaik, C. P. Recognizing the many faces of primate food competition - methods. Behaviour 105, 165–186 (1988)."),[6](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR6 "Koenig, A. Competition for resources and its behavioral consequences among female primates. Int. J. Primatol. 23, 759–783 (2002).").

Within-group scramble competition (WGS) is predicted to create a positive correlation between group size versus daily travel times and distances[7](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR7 "Janson, C. H. & Goldsmith, M. L. Predicting group size in primates - foraging costs and predation risks. Behav. Ecol. 6, 326–336 (1995)."),[8](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR8 "Majolo, B., Vizioli, A. D. & Schino, G. Costs and benefits of group living in primates: group size effects on behaviour and demography. Anim. Behav. 76, 1235–1247 (2008)."). If food is distributed into discrete patches, then large groups may need to visit more patches to obtain the same amount of food per individual[9](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR9 "Chapman, C. A. & Chapman, L. J. Constraints on group size in red colobus and red-tailed guenons: Examining the generality of the ecological constraints model. Int. J. Primatol. 21, 565–585 (2000)."),[10](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR10 "Snaith, T. V. & Chapman, C. A. Red colobus monkeys display alternative behavioral responses to the costs of scramble competition. Behav. Ecol. 19, 1289–1296 (2008)."). When food is more evenly dispersed, individuals in larger groups may have a greater probability of encountering a food site where another group member has already eaten, so they may need to travel farther to find fresh sites[11](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR11 "Gillespie, T. R. & Chapman, C. A. Determinants of group size in the red colobus monkey (Procolobus badius): an evaluation of the generality of the ecological-constraints model. Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 50, 329–338 (2001)."),[12](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR12 "Teichroeb, J. A. & Sicotte, P. Test of the ecological constraints model on ursine colobus monkeys (Colobus vellerosus) in Ghana. Am. J. Primatol. 71, 49–59 (2009).").

If foraging groups advance through their habitat by “pushing forward” the members in the front, then WGS and/or within-group contest competition (WGC) could also contribute to a positive correlation between group size and travel[9](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR9 "Chapman, C. A. & Chapman, L. J. Constraints on group size in red colobus and red-tailed guenons: Examining the generality of the ecological constraints model. Int. J. Primatol. 21, 565–585 (2000)."),[13](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR13 "van Schaik, C. P., van Noordwijk, M. A., Deboer, R. J. & Dentonkelaar, I. The effect of group-size on time budgets and social behavior in wild long-tailed macaques (Macaca-Fascicularis). Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 13, 173–181 (1983)."),[14](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR14 "Chapman, C. A. & Chapman, L. J. Determinants of group size in primates: the importance of travel costs in On the move - how and why animals travel in groups (eds Boinski, S. & Garber, P.) 24–42 (University of Chicago Press, Chicago, 2000)."). WGC can involve aggressive displacement by dominant individuals, or subordinates may move preemptively to avoid such aggression[15](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR15 "Wheeler, B. C., Scarry, C. J. & Koenig, A. Rates of agonism among female primates: a cross-taxon perspective. Behav. Ecol. (2013)."),[16](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR16 "Thouless, C. R. Feeding competition between grazing red deer hinds. Anim. Behav. 40, 105–111 (1990)."). Such competition is typically associated with rank related differences in foraging efficiency and reproductive success[17](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR17 "Vogel, E. R. Rank differences in energy intake rates in white-faced capuchin monkeys, Cebus capucinus: the effects of contest competition. Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 58, 333–344 (2005)."),[18](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR18 "Schülke, O. & Ostner, J. Ecological and social influences on sociality in The evolution of primate societies (eds Mitani, J., Call, J., Kappeler, P. M., Palombit, R. A. & Silk, J. B.) 195–219 (University of Chicago Press, Chicago, 2012)."). WGC may be more intense when foods are small enough to be monopolized and take a long time to consume[19](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR19 "Hirsch, B. T. Costs and benefits of within-group spatial position: A feeding competition model. Quart. Rev. Biol. 82, 9–27 (2007)."),[20](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR20 "Isbell, L. A., Pruetz, J. D. & Young, T. P. Movements of vervets (Cercopithecus aethiops) and patas monkeys (Erythrocebus patas) as estimators of food resource size, density, and distribution. Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 42, 123–133 (1998)."). We will use the term “intragroup feeding competition” to encompass both WGS and WGC.

Between-group contest competition (BGC) may create a negative correlation between group size and travel[7](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR7 "Janson, C. H. & Goldsmith, M. L. Predicting group size in primates - foraging costs and predation risks. Behav. Ecol. 6, 326–336 (1995)."),[8](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR8 "Majolo, B., Vizioli, A. D. & Schino, G. Costs and benefits of group living in primates: group size effects on behaviour and demography. Anim. Behav. 76, 1235–1247 (2008)."). Small groups may travel farther to avoid encounters with large groups, and they may be displaced from food patches where such encounters occur[21](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR21 "Wrangham, R. W. An ecological model of female-bonded primate groups. Behaviour 75, 262–300 (1980)."),[22](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR22 "Markham, A. C., Guttal, V., Alberts, S. C. & Altmann, J. When good neighbors don’t need fences: temporal landscape partitioning among baboon social groups. Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 67, 875–884 (2013)."). BGC is predicted when patches of food are large enough to accommodate an entire group, yet small enough that the group can exclude other rivals[1](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR1 "van Schaik, C. P. The ecology of social relationships amongst female primates in Comparative socioecology: the behavioural ecology of humans and other mammals (eds Standon, V. & Foley, R. A.) 195–218 (Blackwell Scientific Publications, Oxford, 1989)."),[23](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR23 "Sterck, E. H. M., Watts, D. P. & van Schaik, C. P. The evolution of female social relationships in nonhuman primates. Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 41, 291–309 (1997)."). For species with sexual dimorphism, the quality and quantity of males may be more important for winning contests between groups than the total number of members in a group, and feeding competition may overlap with male mating competition[24](#ref-CR24 "Scarry, C. J. Between-group contest competition among tufted capuchin monkeys, Sapajus nigritus, and the role of male resource defence. Anim. Behav. 85, 931–939 (2013)."),[25](#ref-CR25 "Harris, T. R., Chapman, C. A. & Monfort, S. L. Small folivorous primate groups exhibit behavioral and physiological effects of food scarcity. Behav. Ecol. 21, 46–56 (2010)."),[26](#ref-CR26 "Cowlishaw, G. Behavioral patterns in baboon group encounters - the role of resource competition and male reproductive strategies. Behaviour 132, 75–86 (1995)."),[27](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR27 "Richter, C., Heesen, M., Nenadic, O., Ostner, J. & Schülke, O. Males matter: increased home range size is associated with the number of resident males after controlling for ecological factors in wild assamese macaques. Am. J. Phys. Anthropol. 159, 52–62 (2016)."). We will use the term “intergroup contest competition” to refer to BGC while acknowledging a potential influence of mating competition.

The fourth permutation of feeding competition, between-group scramble competition (BGS), is not expected to involve correlations with group size, but may lead to lower foraging efficiency at higher population density[5](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR5 "Janson, C. H. & van Schaik, C. P. Recognizing the many faces of primate food competition - methods. Behaviour 105, 165–186 (1988)."),[28](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR28 "Snaith, T. V. & Chapman, C. A. Primate group size and interpreting socioecological models: do folivores really play by different rules? Evol. Anthropol. 16, 94–106 (2007)."). Increasing population density can reduce the abundance of food, which may intensify the other types of feeding competition[29](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR29 "Isbell, L. A. Contest and scramble competition: patterns of female aggression and ranging behavior in primates. Behav. Ecol. 2, 143–155 (1991)."). For all four types of competition, lower foraging efficiency may involve greater depletion of food sites, and individuals may settle for closer sites with lower quality, resulting in lower food intake rates[8](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR8 "Majolo, B., Vizioli, A. D. & Schino, G. Costs and benefits of group living in primates: group size effects on behaviour and demography. Anim. Behav. 76, 1235–1247 (2008)."),[30](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR30 "Charnov, E. L. Optimal foraging, marginal value theorem. Theor. Pop. Biol. 9, 129–136 (1976)."). To compensate for lower intake rates, as well as the energetic costs of greater travel, individuals may spend more time feeding[28](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR28 "Snaith, T. V. & Chapman, C. A. Primate group size and interpreting socioecological models: do folivores really play by different rules? Evol. Anthropol. 16, 94–106 (2007)."),[31](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR31 "Saj, T. L. & Sicotte, P. Scramble competition among Colobus vellerosus at Boabeng-Fiema, Ghana. Int. J. Primatol. 28, 337–355 (2007).").

A combination of intragroup feeding competition and BGC has been evoked to explain why optimal foraging efficiency occurs at intermediate group sizes[32](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR32 "Markham, A. C., Gesquiere, L. R., Alberts, S. C. & Altmann, J. Optimal group size in a highly social mammal. Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. 112, 14882–14887 (2015)."),[33](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR33 "Stevenson, P. R. & Castellanos, M. C. Feeding rates and daily path range of the Colombian woolly monkeys as evidence for between- and within-group competition. Folia Primatol. 71, 399–408 (2000)."). Intragroup feeding competition can reduce the foraging efficiency for large groups, while BGC can reduce the foraging efficiency of small groups. Furthermore, an upper limit for optimal group sizes has been attributed to infanticide, and a lower limit has been attributed to predation risks[1](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR1 "van Schaik, C. P. The ecology of social relationships amongst female primates in Comparative socioecology: the behavioural ecology of humans and other mammals (eds Standon, V. & Foley, R. A.) 195–218 (Blackwell Scientific Publications, Oxford, 1989)."),[21](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR21 "Wrangham, R. W. An ecological model of female-bonded primate groups. Behaviour 75, 262–300 (1980)."),[34](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR34 "Steenbeek, R. & van Schaik, C. P. Competition and group size in Thomas’s langurs (Presbytis thomasi): the folivore paradox revisited. Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 49, 100–110 (2001)."). Nonetheless, group sizes can vary considerably both within and among species, and the consequences of those variations have not been well quantified[14](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR14 "Chapman, C. A. & Chapman, L. J. Determinants of group size in primates: the importance of travel costs in On the move - how and why animals travel in groups (eds Boinski, S. & Garber, P.) 24–42 (University of Chicago Press, Chicago, 2000).").

Here we investigate the effects of group size on the foraging efficiency of mountain gorillas in the Virunga volcano region. The Virunga mountain gorillas are expected to have weak feeding competition, primarily because their food is abundant[35](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR35 "Watts, D. P. Strategies of habitat use by mountain gorillas. Folia Primatol. 56, 1–16 (1991)."),[36](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR36 "Wright, E. et al. Energetic responses to variation in food availability in the two mountain gorilla populations (Gorilla beringei beringei). Am. J. Phys. Anthropol. 158, 487–500 (2015)."). Distances between patches are small, which limits the extra travel requirements if larger groups must visit more patches[37](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR37 "Watts, D. P. Relations between group size and composition and feeding competition in mountain gorilla groups. Anim. Behav. 33, 72–85 (1985)."),[38](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR38 "Altmann, S. A. Baboons, Space, Time, and Energy. Am. Zool. 14, 221–248 (1974)."). Food sites are numerous and densely distributed within those patches, so extra foraging costs are minimal if some sites have already been depleted, and individuals have little incentive to compete for any particular spot[39](#ref-CR39 "Watts, D. P. Environmental influences on mountain gorilla time budgets. Am. J. Primatol. 15, 195–211 (1988)."),[40](#ref-CR40 "Watts, D. P. Agonistic relationships between female mountain gorillas (Gorilla gorilla beringei). Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 34, 347–358 (1994)."),[41](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR41 "Grueter, C. C. et al. Causes, mechanisms, and consequences of contest competition among female mountain gorillas in Rwanda. Behav. Ecol. 27, 766–776 (2016)."). The Virunga mountain gorillas have been considered unlikely candidates for BGC because intergroup encounters have traditionally been infrequent and intergroup aggression is mainly limited to male mating competition[42](#ref-CR42 "Sicotte, P. Intergroup encounters and female transfer in mountain gorillas - influence of group composition on male behavior. Am. J. Primatol. 30, 21–36 (1993)."),[43](#ref-CR43 "Sicotte, P. Female mate choice in mountain gorillas in Mountain gorillas: three decades of research at Karisoke (eds Robbins, M., Sicotte, P. & Stewart, K.) 59–88 (Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 2001)."),[44](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR44 "Robbins, M. M., Robbins, A. M., Gerald-Steklis, N. & Steklis, H. D. Socioecological influences on the reproductive success of female mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei beringei). Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 61, 919–931 (2007)."). Male mating competition may be more influential than BGC, as groups try to retain females by avoiding encounters with potential rivals, and daily travel distances can be longer after encounters occur[35](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR35 "Watts, D. P. Strategies of habitat use by mountain gorillas. Folia Primatol. 56, 1–16 (1991)."),[45](#ref-CR45 "Watts, D. P. Long term habitat use by mountain gorillas (Gorilla gorilla beringei). 1. consistency, variation, and home range size and stability. Int. J. Primatol. 19, 651–680 (1998)."),[46](#ref-CR46 "Fossey, D. Observations on the home range of one group of mountain gorillas (Gorilla gorilla beringei). Anim. Behav. 22, 568–581 (1974)."),[47](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR47 "Robbins, M. M. & Sawyer, S. C. Intergroup encounters in mountain gorillas of Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, Uganda. Behaviour 144, 1497–1519 (2007)."). Hypothetically, competition among males could also be based on resource defense, but significant evidence has not been found to support such a possibility for gorillas[48](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR48 "Breuer, T. et al. Variance in the male reproductive success of western gorillas: acquiring females is just the beginning. Behav. Ecol. Sociobiol. 64, 515–528 (2010)."),[49](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR49 "Mirville, M. O. The causes and consequences of intergroup interactions in mountain gorillas (Gorilla beringei beringei), PhD Thesis, University of Western Australia, Perth, Australia (2018).").

Previous studies have supported expectations that group size has little influence on the foraging efficiency of this population. Inconsistent results have emerged from analyses of daily travel distance versus group size[35](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR35 "Watts, D. P. Strategies of habitat use by mountain gorillas. Folia Primatol. 56, 1–16 (1991)."),[45](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR45 "Watts, D. P. Long term habitat use by mountain gorillas (Gorilla gorilla beringei). 1. consistency, variation, and home range size and stability. Int. J. Primatol. 19, 651–680 (1998)."). Time spent feeding was significantly longer in larger groups, but the increase was only three percentage points across a three-fold variation in group size[39](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR39 "Watts, D. P. Environmental influences on mountain gorilla time budgets. Am. J. Primatol. 15, 195–211 (1988)."). Dominance rank did also not have a significant effect on the energy intake rates or the proportion of time spent traveling, and rank-related differences in female reproductive success might be due to female quality rather than contest competition[41](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR41 "Grueter, C. Ecol. 27, 766–776 (2016)."),[50](/articles/s41598-018-35255-0#ref-CR50 "Robbins, A. M., Robbins, M. M. & Fawcett, K. Maternal investment of the Virunga mountain gorillas. We predict the opposite patterns if intergroup contest competition predominates. If both types of competition are determining the optimal group size for this population, then foraging efficiency should be highest at intermediate sizes, with lower values for smaller and larger groups (if the probability of winning is based on group size and male number). The p-value remained significant when we removed the largest group from the analysis, however, which suggests that the effects of group size were already leveling off for the other groups. The p-value also remained significant when we removed the smallest group (or any of the other groups). The linear term for group size was also significant in the original model, but not when we removed the quadratic term (p = 0.10).

# Empirical Evidence Review: Dunbar's Number

## Introduction

Dunbar's number — the hypothesized cognitive limit on the number of stable social relationships a human can maintain, conventionally given as 150 — is derived from two interconnected claims. The first is the **Social Brain Hypothesis**: that neocortex size in primates predicts maximum social group size, and that human cognition imposes a specific arithmetic ceiling on our social capacities. The second claim is that human social networks are not merely organized around this single number but exhibit nested layers centered on multiples of five (5, 15, 50, 150, 500, 1,500).

Dunbar's original work traced back to primate brain-body ratios and their correlation with group sizes, later confirmed via neuroimaging in humans. Dunbar argued this ratio "limits how much complexity a social system can handle" (BBC Future, 2019). He applied the number broadly to hunter-gatherer societies, modern workplaces, churches, villages, military organizations, and internet communities worldwide.

This review critically evaluates the empirical evidence surrounding these claims, surveying primatology, anthropology, psychology, sociology, neuroscience, ecology, computational modeling, and economics research. While the concept has been widely influential — Dunbar's original 1998 paper alone has received over 3,000 citations according to Google Scholar — the actual data present nuanced challenges to its universality, methodological rigor, and cultural generalizability. The evidence reviewed falls into several categories: (1) primate studies testing the neuroanatomical foundation of the hypothesis, (2) anthropological and archaeological studies of human group sizes across cultures, (3) empirical tests of network limits in modern humans, (4) ecological critiques offering alternative explanations, (5) computational and mathematical models, and (6) cultural and geographical variation.

---

## 1. Primate Studies: The Neuroanatomical Foundation

### 1.1 Original Findings Supporting the Hypothesis

Dunbar's core claim rested on correlational data showing that primate species with larger neocortex-to-body-size ratios tend to live in larger social groups (Dunbar, 1992). In primates, grooming occupies roughly 20% of waking hours, and both the time available and the duration of each grooming bout scale predictably with group size, suggesting a cognitive rather than purely time-based constraint on relationships.

This foundational approach was subsequently confirmed via MRI neuroimaging in humans (Dunbar et al., 2009), which identified strong positive correlations between neocortex ratio and both offline social circle size and online Facebook friendship count.

Later studies reinforced this pattern: Bennett & O'Connor (2023) found that higher neocortex-to-brain ratios predicted more friends across primate species, while Blomberg et al. (2003) showed phylogenetic signals in primate group sizes aligned with sociality measures including neocortex ratio, body mass, and diet.

### 1.2 The Ecological Alternative: Diet vs. Neocortex

A major challenge to the Social Brain Hypothesis comes from ecological studies arguing that diet — not social complexity — is the primary driver of primate brain evolution. Studies on dietary influences on neocortex evolution suggest that energy-rich diets, particularly fruit consumption and meat-eating, provided the metabolic energy necessary for large brains, while sociality was a secondary correlate rather than a causal factor.

More directly, Grueter et al. (2018) studied mountain gorillas in Rwanda and found that "foraging efficiency decreased with size among most groups, but then began to increase for the largest group," presenting an inverted-U pattern that "provide a new twist on the growing evidence of non-linear relationships between group size and foraging efficiency in primates." This directly challenges the linear predictions of social brain theory: if foraging efficiency, predation risk, and energy competition — not cognitive capacity — determine group size, then neocortex ratios would at best be epiphenomenal.

### 1.3 Great Ape Social Complexity Challenging Neocortex Predictions

Great apes offer particularly interesting tests of the hypothesis because chimpanzees and bonobos live in communities of 50–150 individuals, exceeding human neocortex-based predictions for social group size when adjusted for body mass. These species navigate a complex social landscape that includes shifting alliances, coalition formations, and hierarchical relations — far more cognitively demanding than simple grooming-based cohesion within small groups. This suggests that intelligence can compensate for or exceed what the brain-to-group-size ratio predicts.

### 1.4 Variation Across Primate Species

A survey of primate group sizes reveals staggering diversity:
- **Chimpanzees**: Communities of 50–150, living in fission-fusion units of 3–46 individuals daily
- **Gorillas**: Typically 3–20, with silverback-led groups occasionally reaching 30+
- **Baboons**: Troops ranging from 8 to 145
- **Japanese macaques**: Troops from 8 to 200 in the wild; larger in managed settings
- **Orangutans**: Largely solitary, with adult females and their offspring comprising small social units
- **Spider monkeys**: Multi-level communities of 6–108+ members organized into fission-fusion bands

This immense range — from near solitude to well over 150 — within primates that share relatively homologous cognitive architectures (and whose group sizes are not determined by a universal number) strongly suggests ecological and environmental factors, rather than neuroanatomy alone, drive group composition.

---

## 2. Anthropological and Archaeological Evidence on Human Groups

### 2.1 Hunter-Gatherer Societies

Dunbar argued that hunter-gatherer bands of approximately 25 individuals represent the evolutionary "default" human social unit. Anthropological surveys support this general scale:

- Nomadic forager camps typically contain around 30 people
- Small-scale societies worldwide show a strong tendency toward groups in the range of approximately 20–150 members, with an average near 46 across diverse cultural settings
- These smaller groups are often part of meta-groups or linguistic communities containing up to approximately 500 people

The evidence here is reasonably consistent: small-scale human social organization does cluster around Dunbar's predicted numbers. This represents the strongest category of support for the hypothesis in humans.

### 2.2 Historical and Medieval Settlements

Dunbar identified recurring numerical patterns across historical periods:

- **11th-century English villages**: Average populations approximately 180, remarkably close to 150
- **Anglo-Saxon parishes**: Generally formed around a kin-based nucleus of approximately 30 individuals with an extended range extending up to approximately 290 (consistent with Dunbar's predicted outer layers)
- **Medieval monastic communities**: Frequently organized according to the predicted multi-layered structure
- **Traditional Chinese administrative units**: Often numbered near the theoretical values at 150 and 500

These historical data points provide remarkably consistent support for the numerically specific claims about human group sizes. This is perhaps Dunbar's number's strongest empirical grounding, where actual settlement patterns, parish records, and archaeological data converge on the predicted values.

### 2.3 Military and Organizational Structures

Modern institutions that adopted Dunbar's framework often align with the predictions:

- **Swedish Tax Authority** restructured offices to maintain groups within the 150-person threshold specifically to avoid bureaucratic dysfunction
- **Facebook's corporate structure** intentionally organized around this group size limit (as reported by Facebook's former chief product officer at the 2016 Aspen Ideas Festival)
- **Military organizations**: Platoon/company sizes tend to cluster naturally around these boundaries
- Various manufacturing workplaces and communes self-organize around similar scales

This institutional uptake is remarkable but worth treating as corroborating evidence rather than independent proof — many of these organizations adopted Dunbar's framework *because* it resonated with their observed reality, not because independent pre-existing data confirmed it.

---

## 3. Empirical Tests in Modern Human Populations

### 3.1 Corroborative Evidence

Dunbar and colleagues have conducted numerous empirical studies on contemporary human social networks:

- MRI neuroimaging (Dunbar et al., 2009) identified strong correlations between neocortex ratio and both offline social circle size and online friendship count, with relationships consistent across contexts (offline friends ≈ online friends)
- Internet gaming communities showed identical layered structures as face-to-face interactions ("virtually the same layers")
- Dunbar's own studies found that people who reported higher levels of "virtual sociality" had larger total network sizes but equivalent core-layer sizes compared to those with more traditional offline relationships

### 3.2 Studies Finding Larger or Different Numbers

Not all evidence conforms neatly to 150:

- Some research on varied social groups in the United States found that their social networks clustered **around 290** rather than 150
- Research has shown the distribution of network sizes is often non-normal (not bell-curved), suggesting a few people with massive contact lists may be skewing averages — including those who can afford assistants to manage relationships or outsource emotional labor
- Age-related differences: younger people aged 18–24 maintain larger online social networks than those aged 55 and above, with Dunbar noting their digital relationships may be "just as meaningful as analogue ones" despite the non-physical nature
- Low-income Jamaicans who use extensive mobile phone contact lists — carefully cultivating even casual relationships — regularly exceed 150 contacts

### 3.3 The Role of Outliers

The mathematical concern is fundamental: if network sizes follow a skewed distribution rather than a normal one, "average" may misrepresent the mode. People with outsized social circles (wealthy individuals managing assistants or celebrity-type figures) inflate arithmetic means beyond where most people actually function. This methodological concern significantly undermines claims about a precise universal limit like 150.

---

## 4. Ecological and Environmental Critiques

### 4.1 Foraging Efficiency as Group Size Driver

Grueter et al. (2018) demonstrated that "intermediate sized groups had the lowest foraging efficiency" in mountain gorillas, with both smaller and larger groups performing better — an inverted-U pattern inconsistent with social brain theory's linear predictions. The study attributed this to interplay between within-group feeding competition at moderate scales versus between-group contest competition advantages available only to very large or very small groups. This research explicitly challenges the assumption that cognitive constraints set hard limits on socially organized group sizes.

### 4.2 Environmental Factors in Cross-Cultural Contexts

Research spanning Oaxaca, Mexico and northern Ghana illustrates how cultural adaptation generates different trust circle sizes from the same underlying species:

- **Oaxaca** showed smaller trust circles largely consisting of nuclear relatives, driven by high biological diversity, remote mountainous terrain, and Spanish colonialism's influence on ethnic identities
- **Northern Ghana** exhibited larger trust circles despite scarcer environmental resources that would theoretically favor isolation — cooperation was necessary for survival across ethnic boundaries

Acedo Carmona emphasizes that "focusing on brain size and cognitive limitations may be overly simplistic," since ecological pressures directly shape what social network sizes are adaptive in specific environments.

### 4.3 Predation, Resource Distribution, and Climate as Determinants

Multiple primate studies have shown that environmental adaptations — including foraging ability and capacity to avoid predators — play a more significant role in determining the size of social groups than neocortex size alone. This is particularly relevant for species like orangutans (mostly solitary) versus chimpanzees (highly social), where both share similar brain-to-body ratios but live in dramatically different social contexts dictated by resource availability.

---

## 5. Computational Modelling and Mathematical Analysis

### 5.1 Supportive Models: Cognitive Cost and Information Processing Complexity

Dávid-Barrett & Dunbar (2013) used an agent-based model to demonstrate that "the cognitive demands of coordination impose an upper limit on the size of social group that a species can maintain," showing that progressive increases in information-handling complexity allow organisms to overcome limitations on group size. The model demonstrated three computational strategies corresponding to different levels of information processing, with larger groups requiring increasingly sophisticated data integration methods.

The findings simultaneously support both the social brain hypothesis and the social complexity hypothesis through formalizing a mechanism: managing social relationships requires tracking relational ties at each node level in an expanding network, where the number of connections scales as n × (n − 1) / 2 for a group of n individuals. This exponential growth creates real information-processing burdens that may correspond to observable biological and psychological limits.

### 5.2 Critiques: Under-specified Parameters and Arbitrary Scaling

Several mathematical concerns apply:

- The relationship between neocortical volume and cognitive capacity remains unspecified in many models; the brain is not a simple computational processor
- Dunbar's predicted layering (5, 15, 50, 150, 500) uses powers approximately of 3.7 with consistent multiplication factors, but no formal mathematical derivation proves why these specific integers should emerge
- The model depends on assumed parameters like time investment in grooming and information processing capacity that are themselves estimates, not measured quantities — making predictions sensitive to initial assumptions

### 5.3 Information-Theoretic Concerns

From a broader cognitive science perspective: "We can remember thousands of digits of pi. Or if you're a zoologist, you can remember 6,000 different beetle names or characteristics," as Lind noted regarding the critique of Dunbar's number. When it comes to storing and processing information, there is nothing special about social stimuli." This suggests that domain-general memory rather than social-domain-specific architecture may set the constraints on relationship maintenance, which would complicate any theory that treats social relationships as operating under a single cognitive bottleneck.

---

## 6. Cultural, Historical, and Geographical Variation

### 6.1 WEIRD Population Bias

A critical methodological concern centers on the population studied. Research supporting Dunbar's number is "skewed towards WEIRD (Western, educated, industrialized, rich and democratic) societies." Most evidence comes from:

- European medieval records
- North American organizational studies
- British and American internet user surveys
- European laboratory experiments

When expanded to include non-Western, less-industrialized contexts — such as northern Ghana versus Oaxaca demonstrated above — the picture becomes less uniform. Dunbar's number may "be most applicable for premodern societies or for middle-income groups in contemporary Western societies" but should not be presumed universal without testing across diverse cultural ecologies.

### 6.2 Digital Technology as a Variable, Not a Constant

The internet has fundamentally altered social network dynamics:

- Some argue that online groups like curated digital communities aren't necessarily "intended to last forever," making the pressure for permanence (and thus group-size limit) less relevant
- People can curate and prune connections more easily online, though Dunbar's studies suggest even on platforms like Facebook and Twitter, when relationships are mapped via mutual-friend counts or message frequency, the same layered structure appears
- For those aged under 25 who have never known life without the internet, digital relationships may be functionally equivalent to face-to-face ones, potentially expanding traditional cognitive limits

### 6.3 The Problem of Post-Hoc Fitting

The repeated "success" of Dunbar's number across diverse institutions (military platoons, parishes, offices, villages, online communities) raises a methodological concern: does the theory predict phenomena, or simply describe any phenomenon that happens to have a cluster near approximately 150? Without predictive, prospective validation across independent datasets, repeated post-hoc pattern-matching is weaker evidence than commonly asserted.

---

## 7. Synthesis and Key Limitations of the Evidence

### 7.1 Strengths of the Empirical Base

- Convergent evidence from hunter-gatherer anthropologies (approximately 20–150 members), medieval settlement records (averaging approximately 180 for English villages), military organizational structures, and modern workplace data all independently cluster near Dunbar's predicted boundaries
- The layered structure itself is well-documented across contexts: core layers of ~5, close ties of ~15, meaningful contacts of ~150 appear consistently in both face-to-face studies and digital platforms
- Computationally formalized models provide a mechanistic explanation — tracking social relations requires memory resources that scale super-linearly with group size

### 7.2 Fundamental Limitations

#### Neocortex as an Over-Simplified Predictor
The core assumption that neocortex ratio is the primary constraint on primate social group size has been challenged by ecological models where diet, resource distribution, and inter-group competition are more predictive.

#### The Skewed Distribution Problem
If the actual distribution of network sizes is right-skewed rather than normally distributed, a single number can represent neither typical individual nor population average. Outliers with outsized networks (the super-connected or those who delegate relationship management) distort summary statistics significantly.

#### Geographic and Population Specificity
WEIRD bias means most tests occurred on populations Dunbar's theory was designed to explain. This isn't necessarily invalidation — but it limits the generalizability claims. Cross-cultural testing is sparse by comparison.

#### Temporal Instability
Human social networks are dynamic and evolving, not static. Digital technology changes the architecture of relationship maintenance in ways that may make older estimates less reliable for contemporary populations.

### 7.3 What We Can and Cannot Say

**Empirically supported:**
- Human social networks exhibit layered structure (core layer ~5; close friends ~15; broader ties ~50–150) across contexts studied
- Small-scale human groups (hunter-gatherer bands, medieval villages, military units of various types) tend to self-assemble in numbers generally below 200
- Cognitive resources are genuinely involved in maintaining social relationships — computational models demonstrate limits imposed by information-processing demands

**Empirically uncertain or contradicted:**
- A single cognitive ceiling of specifically approximately 150 applies universally across domains, cultures, and historical periods
- Neocortex ratio is the primary determinant of primate group size (diet and ecology provide better predictions)
- The layered structure follows exact integer multiples because of hardwired neurocognition rather than cultural convention, resource constraints, or emergent organizational dynamics

**Partially supported:**
- Group-living species evolve larger brains to manage social complexity (some support from brain-and-group studies but not sufficient to establish causation)
- Social networks are constrained by time available for relationship maintenance (this constraint is real; when quantified through daily interaction budgets, it generates predicted limits roughly consistent with Dunbar's numbers, though not exactly 150)

---

## Concluding Assessment

Dunbar's number occupies a fascinating position at the intersection of evolutionary psychology, anthropology, neuroscience, and organizational theory. The core insight — that humans have genuine cognitive and temporal constraints on maintaining social relationships — is robustly supported by converging evidence across multiple disciplines. The layered structure of human social networks appears empirically real and cross-culturally documented in many contexts.

However, several critical limitations weaken claims of universality or precision: the theory's foundation on a single neocortex-group-size correlation overlooks ecological determinants that may be causally prior; its supporting datasets are heavily biased toward WEIRD populations; it conflates descriptive patterns with predictive mechanisms; and treating 150 as a precise boundary misrepresents what is actually a range, not an absolute wall.

The most charitable reading of the evidence supports a modified claim: human beings tend to form social organizational clusters within the general ball-park of approximately 50–200 members when unconstrained by external structure or technology, with core layers at smaller scales (5, ~15, and 50). This pattern emerges across many cultures and epochs because it represents a natural balance between cognitive capacity and social benefit — not because there is a hardwired ceiling at any specific number. The ecological, dietary, environmental, and technological factors identified by critics may modify these boundaries in predictable ways but don't eliminate the underlying organizational tendency itself.

Dunbar's contribution was identifying a real pattern that deserved attention; further empirical work should focus on precisely characterizing when, where, and why this organization emerges, and what forces — neural, ecological, cultural, technological — shift those limits up or down.
